The Asian golden clam, Corbicula fluminea, commences its life cycle when fertilised eggs develop into tiny planktonic veliger larvae that drift in the water column before settling. At the moment of hatching, the prodissoconch shell of a newly emerged veliger measures just 0.2 millimeters [Lb = 0.2 millimeters] in shell height at birth, a diminutive size that reflects the lecithotrophic phase during which the larva relies entirely on internal yolk reserves. This initial shell dimension is critical for understanding early growth trajectories, as the transition to planktotrophic feeding occurs soon after eclosion, when the developing ciliated velum becomes active in filtering phytoplankton from the surrounding water. The small size at hatching also imposes high vulnerability to planktonic predators, and only a tiny fraction of larvae survive the first few days of drift before they acquire the ability to seek suitable benthic substrates for attachment. Field surveys indicate that the prodissoconch I stage, corresponding to the embryonic shell formed within the egg capsule, is consistently near this 0.02 cm [Lb = 0.02 cm] value across populations sampled from diverse river systems, suggesting a conserved developmental constraint on egg size in this species.

As the veliger larva grows and approaches metamorphic competence, it undergoes a dramatic transformation that includes the loss of the velum and the development of functional gills and a juvenile foot. The larval-juvenile transition is marked by an allometric shift in shell proportions, with shell height becoming the standard metric for tracking size in post-settlement individuals. Field monitoring of monthly recruitment cohorts in the Potomac River has shown that recently metamorphosed spat measure approximately 0.2 to 0.3 cm in shell height, and these individuals then enter a rapid juvenile growth phase. However, the ultimate shell height (4.8 cm) [Li = 4.8 cm] attained by fully grown adults represents a substantial increase from the tiny hatchling size, reflecting the accumulation of calcium carbonate over several growing seasons. The maximum adult shell height recorded in this species is 4.8 cm [Li = 4.8 cm], a value that is typically reached only after several years of continuous growth under favorable thermal and food conditions. This asymptotic size places Corbicula fluminea among the medium-sized freshwater bivalves, comparable in adult dimensions to many unionid species that occupy similar riverine habitats.

Sexual maturity in Corbicula fluminea is reached at a moderate body size that coincides with the onset of gametogenesis and the first spawning event. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from populations in the San Joaquin River delta indicates that puberty occurs when individuals attain a shell height of approximately 0.6 cm [Lp = approximately 0.6 cm], at which point the first vitellogenic oocytes become visible in the ovaries of females. This shell height at puberty (0.6 cm) [Lp = 0.6 cm] corresponds to a shell length range of roughly 0.6 to 1.0 cm, a size that is typically achieved within the first year of life under the warm, productive conditions found in many invaded habitats. The relatively small size at maturity is a key life-history trait that contributes to the species' invasive success, as it allows individuals to begin reproducing well before they have reached their full adult body size. In contrast, many native unionid mussels delay sexual maturity until they have attained shell lengths exceeding 3 or 4 cm, giving the golden clam a distinct demographic advantage in colonizing new environments. The early onset of reproductive activity also means that even moderate densities of Corbicula fluminea can generate large numbers of offspring within a single year.

Maintained at a stable water temperature of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], individual clams can release approximately 186 fertilised eggs per day [Ri = approximately 186 fertilised eggs per day], a rate that translates into a substantial annual fecundity. This maximum reproduction rate was derived from continuous monitoring of isolated adults over several weeks, during which each clam produced a steady stream of spawned oocytes that were fertilised externally by sperm released simultaneously by nearby conspecifics. The daily output of nearly 200 eggs per individual is remarkable for a bivalve of this body size, and it reflects the energetic investment that the species channels into reproductive effort rather than somatic growth or longevity. In comparison, many freshwater mussels produce far fewer gametes per unit time, often releasing eggs in discrete batches during brief spawning pulses rather than on a continuous daily basis. The continuous spawning strategy of Corbicula fluminea allows it to maintain a constant supply of larvae in the water column throughout the warm season, maximizing the chances of successful settlement on suitable substrates.

The lifespan of Corbicula fluminea is relatively short compared to many other freshwater bivalves, a life-history pattern that is consistent with its high reproductive output and rapid growth rate. Long-term mark-recapture studies of populations in the Ohio River have documented that the maximum lifespan is approximately 6.5 years [am = approximately 6.5 years] when individuals are maintained under non-stressful conditions at 17 °C [T = 17 °C], though most wild clams live for only 2 to 3 years due to predation, parasitism, and seasonal thermal extremes. This lifespan value was recorded from clams held in flow-through aquaria that mimicked natural river conditions, with continuous food supply and stable temperature regulation. In addition to longevity, the relationship between shell height and tissue mass provides valuable information for bioenergetic studies. A detailed morphometric analysis of 150 individuals revealed that the body wet weight at a shell height of 2.7 cm is 12.17 grams , a measurement that serves as a standard reference point for converting length-frequency data into biomass estimates in population surveys. This wet weight at shell height 2.7 cm (12.17 grams)  is typically associated with clams that are in their second or third year of growth, representing a period of active somatic investment before the onset of reproductive senescence.
